NEW DELHI: A 41-year-old woman was allegedly drugged and raped on the pretext of a job opportunity in east Delhi’s Mandawali area, and later blackmailed with a purported video of the incident, police said on Thursday.Police have registered a case in connection with the incident and are conducting raids to apprehend the accused, who is currently absconding, they added.According to news agency PTI, the woman, a resident of Laxmi Nagar, alleged that the accused, Deepak Bansal of Ganesh Nagar, had befriended her around two years ago and promised to help her secure a job.According to the complaint, Bansal approached the woman on March 4 on the pretext of discussing a job and allegedly gave her a substance that rendered her unconscious. He then allegedly raped her, police said.After regaining consciousness, the woman objected to the alleged assault. Bansal then allegedly threatened to circulate a purported video of the incident on social media, police said.The woman also alleged that the accused took her gold bangles, ring and chain and threatened her with dire consequences if she reported the matter to the police.According to the complaint, the accused claimed to have contacts in the police and threatened to throw acid on the woman if she reported the incident.The woman remained silent for several months due to fear but later approached police after allegedly facing continued harassment from the accused.Police said a case was registered against Bansal at Mandawali police station on September 22 under relevant provisions.Teams are conducting raids at possible locations to trace and apprehend the accused, who is currently absconding.The woman has been provided counselling, they said.
Article Summary: A 41-year-old woman was allegedly drugged and raped on the pretext of a job opportunity in east Delhi’s Mandawali area. The woman, a resident of Laxmi Nagar, alleged that the accused, Deepak Bansal, befriended her around two years ago and promised to help her secure a job.

Article Title: Heavy rain lashed as deep depression crosses coast, lay over north coastal Andhra Pradesh, more rains on cards
Article Text:
The system moved west-northwestwards and it was laying over north coastal Andhra Pradesh about 50 km West of Kalingapatnam.





VISAKHAPATNAM: Heavy to very heavy rain lashed at parts of the north coastal Andhra Pradesh between Wednesday night and Thursday morning as deep depression over north Andhra Pradesh coast, moved slowly west-northwestwards and crossed the coast closed to southwest of Kalingapatnam on Wednesday night as a deep depression with speed of 55 kmph to 75 kmph.The system moved west-northwestwards and it was laying over north coastal Andhra Pradesh about 50 km West of Kalingapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), 80 km north-northeast of Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh) and 170 km southwest of Gopalpur (Odisha). The systemis very likely to move northwestwards initially maintaining intensity of deep depression for some hours and thereafter it is very likely to move north-northwestwards and weaken gradually by Friday.Parts of the Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Parvathipuram Manyam, Visakhapatnam, Anakapalle, Alluri Sitharama Raju, Kakinada, Konaseema, East Godavari and West Godavari districts received heavy rainfall on Wednesday. The weather agency forecast that parts of the Vizianagaram, Parvathipuram Manyam, Visakhapatnam, Anakapalle, Alluri Sitharama Raju and Eluru districts will receive heavy rainfall on Thursday (Sep 25).
Article Summary: The system moved west-northwestwards and it was laying over north coastal Andhra Pradesh about 50 km West of Kalingapatnam. Article Title: Gurgaon Murder: Gurgaon man beats live-in partner to death with rolling pin
Article Text:
A 33-year-old man named Akash was arrested for allegedly murdering his live-in partner in Gurgaon





GURGAON: A 33-year-old man was arrested for allegedly murdering his live-in partner by assaulting her with a stick, pipe and rolling pin at their rented house in Dharam Colony, police said.The incident took place on Tuesday when police received information that a woman was lying injured inside a rented house in the Palam Vihar area. A police team reached the spot and found the woman seriously injured and covered in blood. She was taken to a hospital in an ambulance, where doctors declared her dead.Police said the landlord told them that he heard a commotion in the street and, on coming outside, saw the accused, identified as Akash, assaulting the woman. According to the landlord's complaint, Akash hit her on the head before fleeing the spot.A case was registered at Palam Vihar police station on the landlord's complaint. Police subsequently arrested Akash, a native of Bareilly in Uttar Pradesh, from Dharam Colony on Tuesday.During interrogation, police found that the deceased was not Akash's wife, as initially stated in the complaint. The two had allegedly been living together in a live-in relationship since 2020.Akash works as a bus driver in Gurgaon, police said.According to police, the two had an argument over an issue on Tuesday, following which Akash allegedly attacked the woman with a stick, pipe and rolling pin, causing fatal injuries.Police said the three objects allegedly used in the assault were recovered from the spot. The accused was to be produced before a court on Wednesday, while further investigation is underway.
Article Summary: A 33-year-old man was arrested for allegedly murdering his live-in partner in Gurgaon. The incident took place on Tuesday when police received information that a woman was lying injured inside a rented house. She was taken to a hospital in an ambulance, where doctors declared her dead. Police subsequently arrested Akash, a native of Bareilly in Uttar Pradesh, from Dharam Colony.

PATNA: Barely days after a disturbing video of the alleged public harassment of a minor girl in Jamui triggered widespread outrage and police action, another purported incident of a woman being harassed in public has surfaced in Bihar—this time in Samastipur. A video showing a young woman allegedly being surrounded and harassed by a group of youths near an embankment in Jagat Singhpur has gone viral on social media.The Samastipur incident reportedly occurred after the woman and a male acquaintance stopped near the embankment to take photographs. According to preliminary information, some youths present in the area allegedly surrounded the woman and began harassing her. The incident was apparently recorded by someone present at the spot, and the footage was subsequently circulated across social media platforms. However, acting swiftly, the police arrested all four accused after the video came to their notice.The video appears to show the woman standing on the road while several youths surround her. At one point, she reportedly says that she will call her brother, following which the youths respond, "Okay, call him." On the basis of verification, the place of occurrence was identified as the road near the dam situated in village Jagtasinghpur under Karpuri Gram Police Station area,” Singh said.He further stated that the incident is said to be about a week old. The victim seen in the video prima facie appears to be a minor. As the victim could not be immediately identified and keeping in view the sensitivity of the case, the police acted swiftly on the basis of the statement of the police officer and registered a case at Karpuri Gram Police Station under relevant sections of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), POCSO Act and IT Act.Acting promptly, Samastipur Police identified all the accused involved in the case and arrested all four within six hours of receiving the information. Further legal action is being taken, the SP said.The victim prima facie appears to be a minor. Therefore, Samastipur Police has appealed to media persons and social media users not to share any post or content on social media that reveals the identity of the victim or causes mental and social harm to her. Videos of that incident circulated widely online, following which police registered a case and launched a probe. Several accused have since been arrested.

Article Title: ‘Celebrations are not meant for someone to die’: Bombay High Court pushes for decibel caps, ban on firecrackers on roads during festivals
Article Text:
The Bombay high court

Mumbai:

JUDGESPEAK:





Bombay high court on Tuesday said the state govt and other authorities must measure the decibel levels of noise pollution at Ganpati pandals and processions, and take stringent action as per the law, including confiscation of the sound system. It also indicated that it will ban the burning of “highly toxic” and polluting firecrackers during festivals, including Ganeshotsav, on public roads as well as the use of “noise-making metal cylinders” during processions.“Celebrations are not meant for someone to die,” said Justice Girish Kulkarni, who, along with Justice Neela Gokhale, was hearing a suo motu PIL on noise pollution caused by loud music systems and firecrackers on streets during festivals and expressed its primary concern was over the health hazard to citizens exposed continuously to high decibel levels.The authorities must maintain recording and visual meter reading of the on-site noise levels using decibel meters, while mandals must display loudspeaker permissions, else “consequences may follow”, said the bench.The HC said its order, which will be made available late at night, would suggest taking a “good amount’’ as deposit from mandals which will be forfeited for any noise rule violations.Firecrackers are not banned, but no permission is given for them, said state advocate general Milind Sathe, who also informed the HC that while processions are permitted under an exception, mandals also need police nod for sound system.Such permission was subject to compliance of noise pollution rules that do not permit use of loudspeakers after 10pm in public.Sathe said the notification, in fact, covers any instrument that makes noise, which would be subject to the decibel rules.Senior counsel Aspi Chinoy, as amicus curiae appointed by the HC to assist in the matter, along with senior counsel Anil Sakhare and Sanjeev Gorwadkar, for the petitioners from Pune and Thane, respectively, argued how ineffective implementation of rules led to noise pollution during festivals and impinged on the rights of many.“It is possible that with a little bit of will, excesses can be controlled,” submitted Chinoy.Gorwadkar, appearing for a doctor from Thane, said the HC order should apply across festivals and the bench accepted his suggestion. The HC said its main emphasis was to ensure that citizens display a sense of duty and even compassion towards fellow citizens. The bench observed orally, “As a citizen, it is our duty to fellow citizens and it is the duty of the govt to sensitize citizens about this.”Sathe said BMC and police give over 25,000 permissions during Ganeshotsav. To erect a pandal, BMC nod is needed, while procession and loudspeakers are permitted with police nod.Chinoy said, “Police officers must be tasked to prevent noise levels on the spot, not prosecute.” In residential areas, the upper sound limit is 55dB during the day. “No firecracker would be within such a limit,” he said.Justice Kulkarni said perhaps the manufacturers should be asked to disclose on the packaging the decibel levels of each cracker.The HC said the state and authorities must take action. The AG said, “Yes, of course we will.’’The bench said, “Ban firecrackers. Take all measures to stop pollution caused by use of firecrackers. Measure decibel levels and implement laws, including confiscation of sound systems.”The judges orally said, “We would suggest taking a good amount of deposit for loudspeakers. If there are violations, forfeit the systems. There is no dearth of money with these mandals. So much money they spend on these systems.’’The HC praised Nagpur police commissioner for his recent order to ban modified sound systems with DJs and laser beams during festivals from Sept 4 to Nov 1. “Why can’t such a ban be implemented in Mumbai and the rest of Maharashtra as well?” the bench asked.The AG said the Nagpur order is “not a ban’’ and similar order exists for Mumbai issued on Sept 4 which prohibits any assembly of more than 5 persons, any procession and any use of loudspeakers, amplifiers, musical band, bursting of firecrackers in any procession by an assembly from Sept 9 to 23 with an exception to permit assembly and processions to be permitted by zonal DCPs, BMC and their supervisory officers.Sakhare and Gorwadkar were also heard and their concern was that noise levels in residential zones be abided while firecrackers be banned after 10 pm on public streets as law mandates, while advocate Vinay Deshmane from Nashik logged in from there to say his 2009 PIL had led to the state investing almost Rs 99 lakh to ostensibly but decibel reading meters for police stations but most police stations have none.Lawyer said the noise penetrates their homes making it difficult to even stay at home when the processions are on.“ That was our concern. It’s regarding people’s health. What happens to the common man?” Justice Kulkarni said.* We don’t want to be adversarial…we are not preventing the procession...We are concerned about the harmful effect on the health of citizens such noise levels could have...* We want the machinery to be functional. As pointed out by advocates at the bar the machinery is not functional. Merely paying a fine is not good. Action has to be preventive. … can’t first cause damage and affect and thousands of citizens and then pay only a fine* There has to be regulation and apart from that those who use loudspeakers should themselves have some responsibilities towards fellow citizens...we have nothing against processions. But follow the norms...especially when passing a hospital or housing complex...Go slow* You can’t be saying state machinery is helpless. It has come to such a situation and the severity is such that citizens are affected and want action… If we don’t regulate, where do we go? There is already traffic and so many other issues including air pollution. How do you survive in the city? When a procession is on there are people in adjoining buildings, many stranded in cars…what happens to them?* Rule of law has to be maintained
Article Summary: Bombay high court says state govt must measure decibel levels of noise pollution at Ganpati pandals and processions. It also indicated that it will ban the burning of “highly toxic’ and polluting firecrackers during festivals, including Ganeshotsav.

KANPUR: Police arrested drug trader Vineet Minocha’s son Subrat late Wednesday after servant Vishal Gautam alleged that Subrat had offered him Rs 6 lakh to kill his father and instructed him to implicate Subrat’s wife Shalu if caught.Police commissioner Raghubir Lal said the investigation, based on Vishal’s statement and circumstantial and electronic evidence, concluded that Subrat was involved in the murder.Subrat was due to be produced before the court concerned today.Vineet (60) was stabbed to death at his Ratan Orbit apartment in Kalyanpur on Sept 5. HYDERABAD: An 18-year-old nursing student was allegedly strangled to death at her house in a village in Bhadradri Kothagudem district, with police launching a manhunt for a youth accused of persistently pressuring her to marry him after she repeatedly turned down his advances.The victimI Harini (18), a native of Vangannapalem village, was a first year BSc (nursing) student at a private college in Khammam district. Passengers noticed burning smell

Driver, conductor detained

NOIDA: Nine passengers were killed after a bus travelling from Delhi to Mahoba in Uttar Pradesh caught fire on the Yamuna Expressway in Greater Noida late Wednesday night, with an FIR alleging that the driver and conductor ignored repeated warnings from passengers about a burning smell and refused to stop the vehicle.Passengers repeatedly asked the driver to pull over after noticing the smell, but the driver and conductor allegedly told them, "If you want to die, then die; we won't stop the bus," according to the FIR registered on the complaint of a passenger, news agency PTI reported.The FIR was registered at Jewar police station on the complaint of Suneel Kumar, a resident of Hamirpur district. Kumar said he boarded the Raj Kalpana Travels bus from Delhi's Kashmere Gate around 9pm on Wednesday.About 30-35 passengers were on board, according to his complaint.Kumar said the bus reached the 33-km mark on the Yamuna Expressway at around 11.30pm when passengers noticed a burning smell coming from the driver's cabin.The driver allegedly dismissed it as a common smell in the bus and did not stop to check the vehicle, the complaint said.Kumar further alleged that the driver and conductor continued smoking bidis and cigarettes in the cabin before flames suddenly erupted near the driver's seat.Passengers raised an alarm and again asked the driver to stop, but the two allegedly refused, according to the complaint.By the time the bus stopped, the fire had spread through the vehicle and smoke had filled the passenger compartment, Kumar said.He and several other passengers managed to jump out of the bus, while some passengers remained trapped inside.Several passengers suffered burns and were taken to Kailash Hospital in Jewar for treatment. Kumar said he was later informed at the hospital that nine people had been declared dead.Police said the nine passengers died from burns and suffocation.The complaint accused the driver and conductor of "deliberate, gross negligence, rashness and reckless disregard" for passenger safety.It also alleged that passengers' bags, luggage and mobile phones were destroyed in the fire, including belongings kept in the luggage compartment and on the roof of the bus.Police said the driver and conductor have been detained and that further investigation is underway.
Article Summary: Bus travelling from Delhi to Mahoba in Uttar Pradesh caught fire late Wednesday night. Nine passengers died from burns and suffocation, police said. Complaint alleges driver and conductor ignored repeated warnings from passengers about a burning smell and refused to stop the vehicle. Driver and conductor detained by police.

Article Title: Putin's party wins again as expected. So why does Russia still hold elections?
Article Text:
Why does Russia hold elections if Putin is bound to win

Putin’s United Russia party has won 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma.

Does a Russian vote actually matter?

Does the vote count actually matter?

Putin has been in power since New Year's Eve 1999.

So should this be called a gimmick?

1. An election creates a claim of public support

2. It gives the Kremlin a measure of support — even if an imperfect one

Does a Russian vote actually matter?

3. Elections keep political elites in line

4. It gives voters a controlled way to participate

5. Elections can reveal dissatisfaction — but not necessarily change the government

So, is the result meaningless?

Russians went to the polls. The votes were counted. Russian President Putin's party United Russia won again, and comfortably.The result itself was hardly the mystery. The more interesting question is why Russia still goes through the elaborate business of elections when the system makes a genuine change of power extremely unlikely.Because in Russia, an election may not simply be about choosing who governs. It can also tell the Kremlin who is turning up, where support is weakening, which regional leaders can deliver and how well the machinery is working. But first, a simpler question: does a Russian vote actually matter?Putin's ruling United Russia party won 57.83% of the vote, according to Russia's Central Election Commission, with more than 95% of ballots counted. The result gives United Russia 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma, preserving its constitutional majority. In the previous parliamentary election in 2021, the party officially received 49.8% of the vote.The election was also the first parliamentary vote since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Putin had presented it as a test of support for his policies and the war. The Kremlin said the first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in 2022 showed Russians were united around Putin, who has been in power since New Year's Eve 1999.That raises an obvious question: If Russia is widely described as an authoritarian or 'managed' political system, and the Kremlin is not seriously threatened by an opposition party taking power, why bother holding elections at all?It would be too simplistic to say that an individual vote is completely meaningless simply because the ruling party is expected to win. Formally, an individual Russian vote can affect the composition of the Duma in two ways.Half of the 450 seats are distributed through nationwide party-list proportional representation, with a 5% threshold, while the other 225 are elected from single-member constituencies.The weight of an individual vote differs between the two.“In the party-list contest, one vote is a very small part of the national total, although collectively these votes determine 225 seats and can be particularly important when a party is near the 5% threshold,” explained foreign affairs expert Robinder Sachdev. “In a close constituency race, however, a relatively small number of votes can directly determine who wins that seat,” explained foreign expert he added.The 2026 result illustrates how strongly the constituency component can amplify a party's parliamentary strength.United Russia won 355 of the 450 seats, up from 343 in the previous Duma and the party's highest total so far.That gives the party well over the two-thirds threshold in the Duma. It can pass ordinary federal legislation without needing support from other parties and has enough votes for federal constitutional laws and the Duma stage of constitutional amendments.“So an individual vote has limited weight by itself, but aggregated votes — particularly in single-member constituencies — can have a major effect on the parliamentary balance of power,” Sachdev said.In the narrowest sense, yes.Russians cast ballots, those ballots are counted and the resulting numbers determine how parliamentary seats are allocated. United Russia's 57.83% vote share is therefore not simply a number that has no connection whatsoever to voting.But whether voters have a meaningful opportunity to change who exercises power is a different question.Russia's political system has placed significant restrictions on genuine electoral competition. Reuters described the 2026 parliamentary election as taking place in a “tightly controlled political system” in which candidates opposed to Moscow's war in Ukraine have largely been excluded.Several parties besides United Russia are represented in the Duma, but Russia's parliamentary opposition operates within tightly drawn limits, with the major parties generally supporting Putin on key issues, including the war in Ukraine.According to the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), Yabloko, a liberal party that opposed the Ukraine war and called for a ceasefire, was excluded from the federal parliamentary contest. CEPA said Yabloko's support among decided voters had risen to about 6% in the weeks before the election, compared with 1.2% in the 2021 election. Meanwhile, Putin critic Nikolai Bondarenko had already been barred from standing.Not quite.Even when the broad political outcome is predictable, elections can serve several purposes for an authoritarian political system.Sachdev said elections provide formal electoral legitimacy while allowing the leadership to demonstrate a measurable level of public participation and support.“Elections also help manage the political system itself,” Sachdev said, adding that they provide opportunities to renew parliament, accommodate different groups within the governing establishment and assess the performance of regional political organisations and officials.They also provide information.“The Kremlin may already have extensive polling and administrative data, but an actual election reveals the geography, intensity and organisational strength of support across the country,” he said.In other words, the Kremlin does not necessarily need an election to discover who rules Russia. It can use an election to find out how well the political machine is functioning.The first and most obvious purpose is legitimacy.The Kremlin can point to an electoral result and say that millions of Russians participated and that the governing party received a majority of votes.That does not settle the question of whether the election was free and fair. But politically, the existence of an official vote gives the government a concrete result with which to demonstrate public backing.This election is particularly significant because it took place during the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin has an interest in demonstrating that the war has not produced a political revolt at home.Sachdev said the election allows the Russian leadership to “demonstrate a measurable level of public participation and support”, even if the broader political outcome is predictable.That distinction is important. An election can provide a government with an official measure of participation without necessarily providing an unrestricted contest for political power.This is where the question of whether votes “count” becomes more complicated.Even in a tightly controlled election, authorities can learn something from participation. How many people turn out? Where is turnout unusually low? Which regions deliver particularly strong support? Where does United Russia perform worse than expected? Are local officials able to mobilise their populations?These are valuable pieces of information for an authoritarian government.A 2021 Carnegie analysis described Russian parliamentary elections as functioning less as contests over who would govern and more as a mechanism for measuring and demonstrating support for Putin's system.Sachdev said an election provides a different kind of information from opinion polls, intelligence reports or administrative data because it “tests behaviour and administrative capacity under real conditions.”“Turnout, abstention, regional variations and the performance of individual candidates can reveal where support is strong, where enthusiasm is weaker, and how effectively governors and local political organisations are able to mobilise voters,” he said.Moreover, information moving upwards through a political hierarchy can be filtered, because officials may have incentives to report favourable results to their superiors.Sachdev said an election can therefore provide an additional dataset against which those reports can be assessed. “Political-science research describes this as a ‘fire alarm’ function of elections,” he said.So the election does not simply measure public opinion. It gives the Kremlin a regional picture of both political sentiment and the effectiveness of the state and party machinery in mobilising voters.There is another audience for Russian elections that is often overlooked: the people inside the system.An election allows governors, mayors, party officials and other local power brokers to demonstrate that they can deliver the results expected by Moscow.Carnegie has described regional elections in Russia as an “initiation ritual” for governors and local elites — an opportunity for them to demonstrate control over their territories.Sachdev said regional leaders are expected not only to administer their territories but also to maintain political stability and demonstrate an ability to mobilise electoral support.Research on Russian regional politics has found that United Russia has historically performed better where governors command effective political organisations and local networks, he said.This means an election can function almost like an internal performance review. If a governor produces the desired result, it demonstrates political control.If a region suddenly records unexpectedly weak support for the ruling party, that can raise questions in Moscow about the governor's popularity, the effectiveness of the regional administration, the strength of the local party organisation or underlying economic and social dissatisfaction.An unexpectedly poor result would not automatically lead to a governor's removal. But, Sachdev said, electoral underperformance “can weaken a regional leader's standing with the federal centre” and become one factor in subsequent decisions about appointments, tenure or political advancement.So even if the Kremlin already knows which party will dominate parliament, the election can tell it how effectively its political network is operating below the national level.There is also a social function.Russia's government does not necessarily want every citizen to become politically disengaged. Voting gives people a formal mechanism for expressing preferences, even if the range of choices is restricted.The question is not necessarily whether the Kremlin believes Russians are choosing between two equally viable governments.Rather, elections can allow the system to channel political participation without allowing that participation to threaten the basic distribution of power.Sachdev said elections also help “renew the composition of parliament” and accommodate different groups within the governing establishment.This means that even where the election does not pose a serious threat to the ruling political system, it can still play a role in determining which individuals and factions occupy positions within that system.This is perhaps the most counterintuitive part.A controlled election can still contain information about dissatisfaction.People can abstain. They can spoil ballots. They can vote for smaller parties or candidates. They can use whatever limited electoral choices are available to signal disagreement.Russia's political opposition has previously tried to use elections tactically to weaken United Russia, even when it could not realistically replace the Kremlin.But the ability to express dissatisfaction and the ability to translate that dissatisfaction into a change of government are two different things which is why the Kremlin may tolerate a certain degree of electoral competition while drawing firm limits around the political system.Not necessarily.The official vote count is meaningful as a description of what Russia's electoral authorities say happened. But the number cannot be read in isolation as a straightforward measure of Russians' freely expressed political preferences.The composition of the ballot matters. So does who was permitted to campaign, what political views could be openly expressed, the degree of media access available to competing forces, turnout and the broader electoral environment.This creates the central paradox of Russia's elections - The votes can be real without the contest being genuinely competitive. A Russian voter can make a choice. But the political system determines, to a significant extent, which choices are available in the first place. That is why the 57.83% figure needs to be read carefully. It is an official electoral result, but it is not equivalent to saying that 57.83% of all Russians freely chose Putin's political system.
Article Summary: Putin's ruling United Russia party won 57.83% of the vote, with more than 95% of ballots counted. The result gives United Russia 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma, preserving its constitutional majority. The election was also the first parliamentary vote since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Article Title: Delhi's parks, streets, shops: Nowhere feels safe for these girls
Article Text:
Delhi recorded 13,396 crimes against women, including 1,058 rape cases, in 2024.

Experts highlight gaps in prevention and surveillance

Security at Delhi parks under scanner

Four cases, four locations, same questions

4 incidents, 4 locations, same safety concerns

Delhi’s numbers show it is not a two-week problem

The difference between response and prevention





In a span of 14 days, four cases involving minor girls have put Delhi's safety record under the scanner again. The circumstances of the incidents vary, but collectively they highlight a familiar problem: children and young women are still vulnerable in places that shouldn't necessarily be hard to secure – a neighborhood shop, a city street, an open area and a public park.The latest case, where a 17-year-old was allegedly gang-raped by men posing as policemen in Kalkaji's Aastha Kunj Park (South Delhi), has brought the concern sharply back into focus.The four cases reported since Sept 10 involved girls aged between six and 17 years old. In Swaroop Nagar, a 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped and killed after she went to meet a teenage acquaintance. Four people including three juveniles have been arrested.An 11-year-old was allegedly raped inside a shop in Sadar Bazaar when she went to buy stationery. A six-year-old was allegedly sexually assaulted on the Deshbandhu Gupta Road while a 17-year-old was allegedly attacked by three men claiming to be police personnel in South Delhi.What is striking is not one common suspect or a common method, but the variety of circumstances in which the girls were allegedly targeted.One incident took place after a meeting with an acquaintance of the victim, one in a commercial premises, one in a public locality and the latest in a park.That makes safety a bigger question than policing isolated hotspots. It raises questions about surveillance, lighting, access control, community vigilance and how quickly warnings are acted upon.The latest NCRB data gives the bigger picture. Among the 19 metropolitan cities covered in the report, Delhi reported the highest absolute numbers with 13,396 cases of crime against women including 1,058 cases of rape in 2024. The capital also registered 7,662 crimes against children in 2024, the highest among metros again. Some categories saw a slight dip in figures but the volume remains large.One more important number in the latest data — Delhi Police said the city recorded 1,901 rape cases in 2025 as against 2,076 in 2024 and 2,141 in 2023.Police also said that in 2025, 95% of murder cases were solved and 97% of rape cases were solved. One important distinction is clear from these figures: the investigation and arrests after a crime can be robust but do not answer the harder question of how vulnerable places and potential victims can be protected before an offense takes place.There has been a rapid response to the latest cases. In Kalkaji case, police said all three accused were arrested within around 12 hours after CCTV footage and technical inputs were examined.One suspect was injured in an encounter. In the Swaroop Nagar case, police examined footage of over 50 CCTVs and traced a suspicious tempo to zero in on the suspects. These investigations show the importance of the surveillance and quick police response following the commission of an offense.But the bigger test of safety comes before the crime. The Aastha Kunj case has already highlighted the gaps in CCTV coverage, lighting and security around the park.The Lady Shri Ram (LSR) college decision to hold classes online after the incident shows how quickly a crime in a public space can change everyday life. So the question for Delhi is not just how well suspects are caught, but whether known vulnerabilities are being fixed before they turn into crimes.Four cases in 14 days cannot be considered a new trend in Delhi’s crime rate. Each case has to be evaluated on its own. But they do give a sense of the different ways that minors can fall into trouble in the city.The arrests are important, so do the FIRs and the probes. But the real test of safety will be whether Delhi can ensure that its neighborhoods, streets, commercial areas and public spaces are safe enough that police intervention is required before, rather than after, a child becomes a victim.
Article Summary: Delhi recorded 13,396 crimes against women, including 1,058 rape cases, in 2024. The capital also registered 7,662 crimes against children in 2024, the highest among metros again. Delhi Police said the city recorded 1,901 rape cases in 2025 as against 2,076 in 2024 and 2,141 in 2023.

Article Title: Delhi Aastha Kunj park gang-rape accused carried condom in pocket, reveals probe
Article Text:
Investigators are examining whether the three had been involved in similar incidents earlier that went unreported.

Accused 'washed' clothes after incident

Phones sent to FSL for data retrieval

Police had alerted DDA about park security

(The victim's identity has not been revealed to protect her privacy as per Supreme court directives on cases related to sexual assault)





NEW DELHI: Police investigating the alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl at Aastha Kunj Park in south Delhi are examining whether the three accused had targeted other vulnerable couples in the past, while investigators are also probing the alleged destruction of evidence after Monday evening’s incident.Police sources said Asif, one of the accused, was allegedly carrying a pistol and a condom in his pocket when he entered the park, followed by two brothers, Hemant Singh and Mukesh Singh.Investigators are examining whether the three had been involved in similar incidents earlier that went unreported.The police are pursuing the angle as the three men were known to frequently hang around the park during late hours. So far, investigators have not found any previous complaints against them.The girl and her friend were sitting on a bench when the three men allegedly approached them while posing as policemen in plain clothes, police said.After allegedly intimidating the teenagers, they took the boy around 200 metres away and allegedly slapped and threatened him. The girl was then taken to a secluded and dark stretch of the park, where the three men allegedly took turns raping her, police sources said.The girl was allegedly threatened against disclosing the incident to anyone.Investigators are also examining what the accused allegedly did after leaving the park.According to news agency ANI, police said Hemant and Mukesh allegedly returned home after the incident and washed everything, including their lower garments, in an attempt to destroy evidence. They also allegedly deleted their search history.Police are examining these actions as part of the investigation into possible attempts to destroy or remove evidence.Investigators have also examined the mobile phones of the accused.Police sources said they found “objectionable material”, including videos, on Asif’s phone. Some data was allegedly deleted from the phones of Hemant and Mukesh.The phones have been sent to the Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) to retrieve the deleted data, sources said.Investigators are examining the digital evidence as part of the probe into the alleged crime and to establish the movements and activities of the accused.The incident has also brought scrutiny on security arrangements at Aastha Kunj Park. The Delhi Development Authority (DDA), which maintains the park, is facing criticism over the lack of CCTV cameras inside the premises.Police have pointed out that there were no CCTV cameras inside the park and said they had alerted the DDA at least three times about security concerns since 2025.DDA sources said its horticulture department had also written multiple letters over the past year seeking increased patrolling at the park.A DDA official said nine security guards were deployed during each shift at strategic locations, along with supervisory and patrolling arrangements.Police are continuing to investigate the alleged rape, the accused’s movements before and after the incident, possible earlier complaints involving them and the alleged attempts to destroy evidence.
Article Summary: Police investigating alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl at Aastha Kunj Park in south Delhi. They are examining whether the three accused had targeted other vulnerable couples in the past. Investigators are also probing the alleged destruction of evidence after Monday’s incident.

Article Title: Smoke, screams and panic: Passengers recall frantic escape after bus catches fire on Yamuna Expressway
Article Text:
Passengers on a bus that caught fire on the Yamuna Expressway experienced a chaotic escape.





NOIDA: Passengers on board a bus that caught fire on the Yamuna Expressway near Noida International Airport on Thursday morning described a chaotic and difficult escape as thick smoke engulfed the vehicle.Speaking to ANI, a passenger said they were asleep when someone alerted them that the bus had caught fire. “After I fell asleep, someone woke me up saying the bus had caught fire, and we all scrambled to get out,” the passenger said.Describing the escape as difficult, the passenger said there was heavy smoke inside the bus and passengers were forced to get out in a state of panic. “It was not an easy situation to escape from; there was a lot of smoke. We somehow managed to get out in a state of panic. The bus was packed with passengers,” the passenger said.Another passenger said they were asleep when someone banged on the door. By the time they woke up, a crowd had gathered and passengers were scrambling to get out.“I didn't pick up any of my belongings; I didn't even put on my shoes. I just grabbed my phone and stepped out,” the passenger said, adding that the rush to escape led to passengers shoving one another.The passenger said someone eventually pulled them out of the bus. “It was so smoky that nothing was visible; people were suffocating inside. Very few managed to escape, only those who could push their way out amidst the shoving,” the passenger said.The passenger said several people were still behind when they managed to get out. “There were quite a few people behind me who probably couldn't make it out, as I myself got out quite late,” the passenger said.The incident left passengers in panic as the packed bus quickly filled with smoke, making it difficult for those inside to find their way out.
Article Summary: Passengers on board a bus that caught fire on the Yamuna Expressway near Noida International Airport on Thursday morning described a chaotic and difficult escape. One passenger said there was heavy smoke inside the bus and passengers were forced to get out in a state of panic. The rush to escape led to passengers shoving one another.

Article Title: Minor girl raped at Delhi hotel by social media friend; accused on the run
Article Text:

(The victim's identity has not been revealed to protect her privacy as per Supreme court directives on cases related to sexual assault)

(With agency inputs)





NEW DELHI: A minor girl was allegedly raped at a hotel in north Delhi’s Wazirabad area by a man who had befriended her through social media, police said.The incident took place at a hotel under the jurisdiction of Wazirabad police station. Police said a case has been registered under relevant provisions of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act and other sections.According to police, the girl and the accused, both residents of Wazirabad, had become acquainted through social media.The accused allegedly took the minor to the hotel on the pretext of their friendship and raped her there, police told news agency PTI.After the incident, the girl returned home and informed her family about the alleged assault. Her family subsequently approached the police, following which the girl was medically examined and her statement was recorded, they said.Based on the girl’s statement and medical examination, Wazirabad police registered a case against the accused, who has been absconding since the incident.Police teams have been conducting raids at possible locations to trace and apprehend the accused, officials said.The police are also examining the circumstances under which the minor was allowed entry into the hotel. Investigators are checking the hotel's register, CCTV footage and other records as part of the probe, they said.
Article Summary: A minor girl was allegedly raped at a hotel in north Delhi’s Wazirabad area by a man who had befriended her through social media. Police said a case has been registered under relevant provisions of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act and other sections.
